item.title: The Lindsay Clancy Trial: An Update
item.description:
Law and Crime

The Lindsay Clancy Trial: An Update

Five psychiartic experts opined on Ms. Clancy's sanity. But what was missing?

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Experts failed to assess Clancy's thoughts during the killings, which are crucial for insanity.
  • Two prosecution experts interviewed Clancy together, compromising independent evaluations.
  • Defense expert saw Clancy soon after the killings but didn't directly link her delusions to the acts.

After an emotionally charged five-week trial, jurors were unable to unanimously decide whether Ms. Clancy murdered her three children with conscious premeditation or was legally insane. Judge William Sullivan declared a mistrial after the jury foreperson reported they were deadlocked.

The defense called two experts and the prosecution three rebuttal experts. Forensic psychologist Dr. Paul Zeizel was the first defense witness. His evaluation began only 11 days after the killings. He interviewed Ms. Clancy 45 times. Over 35 hours, he reconstructed Ms. Clancy’s depression, mood instability, and postpartum psychosis. She believed strangers could read her thoughts. She felt compelled to kill the children and herself. During a phone call to her husband, Dr. Zeizel heard her tell him that a male voice commanded her to kill the children. He diagnosed Ms. Clancy with postpartum psychosis and bipolar II disorder, concluding that a mental disorder impaired her ability to appreciate the moral wrongfulness of her actions.

Defense forensic psychiatrist Dr. Phillip Resnick, an expert on maternal filicide, examined Ms. Clancy four months after the killings for three hours. He diagnosed severe depression, bipolar II disorder, suicidal intent, and postpartum psychosis, manifested by a command hallucination. She was preoccupied with her children’s welfare, believing they could not live without her, which is characteristic of altruistic filicide. He described her as a puppet on a string and concluded that impaired judgment and reality testing contributed to the killings.

The prosecution called three experts. Two of them, psychologist Dr. Kirk Heilbrun and psychiatrist Dr. Avram Mack, interviewed the defendant together and apart for about 13 hours over three days, three years after the killings.

Dr. Heilbrun concluded that Ms. Clancy was suicidal and did not want to leave her children behind. Although he characterized the killings as “altruistic filicide,” he concluded her state of mind did not prevent her from recognizing her actions were wrong.

Dr. Avram Mack opined that Ms. Clancy suffered major depression, but not postpartum psychosis. Although acknowledging a hallucination, he noted this does not necessarily establish a psychotic disorder. He concluded she retained the ability to understand the wrongfulness of her actions.

Psychiatrist Dr. Gregory Saathoff, the third prosecution witness, opined that Ms. Clancy was purposeful in her suicide plan, evidenced by a normal conversation with her husband before the stabbings. He believed her filicidal motivations were not caused by a one-time command hallucination, which is rare, and concluded she was sane at the time of the killings.

What I found most illuminating about the expert testimony was not what was said, but what was missing: a careful inquiry into Ms. Clancy’s emotions and thoughts while the killings took place. Among the experts, Dr. Zeizel was in the unique position to closely examine the defendant’s thinking before it was potentially contaminated by time and defensive reasoning, as he examined her days after the killings. During his testimony, Dr. Zeizel outlined her thinking difficulties, such as her reported hallucination, and her delusional belief that others were reading her mind. However, he did not provide direct evidence of a connection between her thinking distortions and the strangulations. This nexus is crucial, as the assessment of her thoughts at the time of the killings is the required cognitive prong of the insanity defense, with mental disease being the other prong. Her thought processes and content during the killings are decisive, as the law states that a defendant must lack a substantial capacity to understand that the act was against the law or common moral principles.

article continues after advertisement

Did Dr. Zeizel ask Ms. Clancy directly about her thoughts when she was strangling the children? Did he ask, “What was going through your mind” during the killings, for instance? She commented to a hospital chaplain immediately after the stabbings, “I am so glad my children are safe." What exactly was she thinking about the strangulations when she made that comment? Were the killings in response to a burning resentment of her children, as the prosecution alleged, or was she driven to protect them from some sinister fate? A probing exploration of her thinking might have led to a linkage between her thinking and its degree of reality distortion that is crucial to the insanity defense.

Experts are required to make independent decisions regarding a defendant’s mental state during an insanity evaluation. Two of the prosecution witnesses, Dr. Heilbrun and Dr Mack, interviewed Ms. Clancy together, thus compromising their autonomous decision-making. It is more accurate to say they jointly proffered one opinion on Ms. Clancy’s sanity.

Dr. Heilbrun characterized the killings as an act of altruistic filicide, but nonetheless opined that Ms. Clancy was sane. This strikes me as odd. If she believed (cognitive prong) that the killings were humane acts, a description of her good-enough rational thoughts at the time of the crimes, on which he based his opinion, should have been provided.

Dr. Gregory Saathoff emphasized Ms. Clancy's ability to carry on a normal conversation before the stabbings, and that a one-time command hallucination is rare. All true. But not probative. One-time command hallucinations are rare with schizophrenic illnesses, but symptoms of postpartum psychosis are more unpredictable. And delusional people can act normally: it is their disordered inner life that is problematic. Again, what was she thinking at the time of the killings?

I recognize that the testimony offered during the trial by the experts might have been limited by the questions posed by the attorneys.

Still, 11 of 12 jurors found Ms. Clancy to be insane. The one holdout, according to the jury foreman, expressed the belief that he had reasonable doubt about Ms. Clancy’s criminal responsibility, but refused to acquit. In Massachusetts, the burden of proof is on the prosecution to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the defendant was criminally responsible, i.e., sane, which is why the jury foremen complained to Judge Sullivan that the juror was refusing to follow the law. The judge disagreed.

article continues after advertisement

My prediction: In lieu of another trial, the prosecution will reach a plea agreement with the defense.

item.title: What Will You Do to Escape Uncertainty?
item.description:
Anxiety

What Will You Do to Escape Uncertainty?

Why not knowing can drive us to make decisions we may later regret.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety can carry useful information about what uncertainty threatens or means to us.
  • Some people tolerate uncertainty better than others, affecting how they respond to anxiety.
  • Understanding your anxiety can help you make better decisions, instead of simply seeking relief.
Source: Kyle Glenn / Unsplash

What is your relationship to uncertainty? For most of us, ambiguity serves as the basis of anxiety, which is a categorically uncomfortable feeling. How far will you go to escape the anxiety associated with not knowing?

Some of us can remain in limbo indefinitely. In contrast, others will act to exit the state of not knowing, often making bad or impulsive decisions to regain clarity and escape ambiguity.

Let's look at two different examples of managing uncertainty I have seen in my work.

Chloe is a lawyer in her early thirties and was six months into dating someone she thought would become her long-term partner when she noticed a subtle shift: he changed the cadence of his text responses and seemed distracted on dates. She began seeking reassurance from him that the relationship was “ok.” Despite his affirmations of love and support, she had difficulty with not knowing where she stood. To escape her intense anxiety, she ended the relationship, which was very painful, but offered immediate relief from the uncertainty.

Now let’s look at Lena, also in her thirties. She works for a large media company and was seeing me to better understand her relationship patterns. At her company, layoffs and restructuring happened regularly. Employees were offered an attractive layoff package, but the company offered no reassurance about what the future held for those who didn't take it. Office rumors swirled about mergers with another company and more layoffs with no severance.

Lena seriously contemplated taking the layoff offer, but she also knew the job market was competitive for her role. Despite her family and friends encouraging her to take the offer, she chose to live with the uncertainty, even if it meant she might be in a worse position later. For eight months, she watched as her co-workers took the offer, and then people were indeed laid off, but she was not.

What allowed Lena to remain in uncertainty while Chloe needed to resolve it?

For Chloe, it was better to escape the uncertainty of the situation with the clarity of a breakup than to sit in her discomfort. However, she will never know what might have happened if she managed her anxiety. I helped her gain a deeper understanding of her childhood, family of origin, and how her lack of self-awareness led to sometimes impulsive decisions.

When Lena kept showing up to work, she chose to face her uncertainty and understand it better. We could see the impact her unwaveringly supportive parents had on her tolerance for uncertainty, which gave space for her to learn ways of managing anxiety.

Neither woman's history entirely explains how they responded to ambiguity, but understanding themselves better helped each of them make sense of their relationship to uncertainty.

Starting in the 1990s, researchers developed the Intolerance of Uncertainty Scale (IUS). Questions like “Uncertainty makes life intolerable” and “Being uncertain means that I lack confidence” are rated on a 1-5 scale. They found that higher intolerance of uncertainty is associated with greater anxiety and worry. Subsequent research suggests that when people have difficulty tolerating uncertainty, they may try to reduce it through behaviors such as reassurance-seeking, checking, or avoidance.

What is your relationship to “what if”? If you find yourself making decisions based on worst-case scenarios, you may be harming yourself in the service of escaping uncertainty.

Rollo May was an American psychologist and psychotherapist who became a leading figure in existential psychology in the United States. Influenced by European existential thinkers such as Kierkegaard, he argued that anxiety isn't necessarily pathological: some anxiety is an inevitable consequence of being human, of having freedom, making choices, confronting uncertainty, and knowing that life is finite.

In his 1977 book, The Meaning of Anxiety, he describes the difference between normal anxiety, which can be faced and used constructively, and neurotic anxiety, in which attempts to avoid or suppress anxiety constrict a person's life.

To him, psychological health doesn't require eliminating anxiety; it requires developing the capacity to live, choose, and act despite uncertainty. And even to thrive.

Perhaps anxiety is not simply a symptom to resist; it’s a feeling state that can be managed by accepting it as part of life. If you can do that, there are many paths towards healthier ways of living.

Consider a few interventions to reframe excessive worry about events outside of your control.

Distinguish danger from uncertainty. Ask yourself: What is actually threatening me right now, and what simply remains unknown? If you can get closer to reflecting what the threat is, you might realize it stems from historical personal events, and it may be more tolerable once you understand the connection. For Chloe, despite breaking up her relationship, she was ultimately able to understand that her anxiety was based on her mother leaving her father and not the events in her relationship. Armed with this knowledge, she was able to manage her anxiety better when confronted with uncertainty in her future.

Allow anxiety to carry information. If you sense anxiety in an uncertain situation, try to understand it better before you make a potentially regrettable decision. Relationship uncertainty may reveal how much attachment matters; career anxiety may raise questions about identity or worth. If you pay attention, you may realize the work is to understand yourself better, so you make better decisions. Lena recognized that she could manage her future uncertainty because she had done the hard work of understanding herself.

Next time you feel on the verge of making a decision based on escaping uncertainty, ask yourself: will it be worth the trade-off?

item.title: How to Build Hope When Your Relationship Feels Stuck
item.description:
Relationships

How to Build Hope When Your Relationship Feels Stuck

Hope grows when we see that our actions can make a difference.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Relationship hope grows when partners see their behavior can positively influence what happens between them.
  • Self protective responses can reinforce relationship patterns that leave partners feeling hurt and powerless.
  • Expressing vulnerability beneath anger or defensiveness gives a partner something different to respond to.
  • Having agency means recognizing our power to influence what happens next.

By the time many couples come to therapy, they are exhausted. They may still love each other deeply, yet find themselves returning to the same argument, the same hurt, and the same sense that nothing they do seems to make a difference.

That is often when hopelessness sets in.

But hope in relationships is not something we simply have or lose. It is something we can build. And an important part of building hope is experiencing that our own behavior can make a difference in what happens between us.

We cannot control our partner. But we can become curious about the patterns we participate in and what happens when we show up differently.

When the Pattern Becomes the Problem

Many couples become caught in a familiar cycle.

One partner feels criticized and becomes defensive or pulls away. The other experiences that distance as rejection and reaches harder, perhaps becoming more critical or demanding. The more one pursues, the more the other withdraws.

Before long, both people are protecting themselves, even though neither wants to be there.

When something important feels at risk, such as our connection to someone we love or our sense of being valued, we naturally become self protective. The problem is that the ways we protect ourselves can unintentionally bring about the very response we fear.

Recognizing this shifts the question from “Who is at fault?” to “What keeps happening between us, and what happens if I respond differently?”

The Power of Showing Up Differently

Consider a partner who feels increasingly hurt that her partner rarely asks questions about her experience.

At dinner one night, she decides to see how long it will take him to ask her a question. She waits. Internally, she keeps track. Dinner passes without a question.

By the end, she is furious. She blows up at him. He feels attacked and becomes defensive.

Now they both have more evidence for the stories they already carry. She thinks, “See, he’s self absorbed and doesn’t care about me.” He thinks, “Nothing I do is good enough for her. I'm just going to get yelled at”

What neither has been able to hear is what lies underneath her anger: I want to feel that you are interested in me. I want to know that my experience matters to you.

In therapy, she might practice bringing that more vulnerable experience forward: “When you don’t ask me questions about my day, I start to feel like I don’t matter to you. I really long for you to be curious about my experience.”

That gives her partner something different to respond to. Instead of hearing an accusation, he has a better chance of hearing the hurt and longing underneath it. He, in turn, can work on asking questions and showing more interest in her experience.

This sounds simple, but it can be surprisingly difficult. Changing our own behavior can feel deeply unfair when we are the one who feels hurt. A self righteous part of us may insist, “Why should I have to change when my partner is the one hurting me?”

Agency asks something difficult of us. It asks us to distinguish between being responsible for the problem and having the power to influence what happens next. We can acknowledge that our hurt is real while also becoming curious about whether the way we protect ourselves is helping us get what we most long for.

This Is Where Hope Begins

Imagine that the following week, she notices him asking more questions.

Something important has happened. The relationship is not suddenly fixed, but she has had a new experience: When I showed up differently, something between us changed.

That is a powerful source of hope.

Hope is not simply telling ourselves that things will get better. It grows when we experience that our actions can have a positive impact. We begin to see ourselves as participants in the relationship rather than powerless observers waiting for our partner to change.

Sometimes that means staying present instead of withdrawing. Sometimes it means softening instead of defending. Sometimes it means making a vulnerable request instead of expressing the need through criticism.

None of this guarantees that a partner will change. Relationships require participation from both people, and one person cannot repair a relationship alone. But experiencing that we have some capacity to influence what happens next can loosen the helplessness that keeps couples stuck.

Creating Something Different

The goal is not to become a couple who never falls into an old pattern. It is to recognize the pattern sooner, understand what is happening underneath it and become better at finding your way back to each other.

Couples therapy can help partners see their protective responses and take the risk of showing more of what lies underneath them.

Hope does not come from believing everything will suddenly become easy. Hope grows through the experience that something different is possible and that how we show up can help create that difference.

item.title: Stop Blaming Kids for Technology Designed to Capture Them
item.description:
Adolescence

Stop Blaming Kids for Technology Designed to Capture Them

It's not screens. It's the slot machine in their pocket, and adults must fix it.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • California’s new social media law targets addictive design for kids under 16, not screen time or content.
  • Constant online stressors keep the nervous system from returning to baseline, stacking stress
  • Teens' reward and social brain systems are highly responsive, which makes addictive design especially risky.
  • Kids can't police their own online safety. That duty belongs to companies and the adults entrusted with them.

For two decades, the debate about kids and technology has circled around two questions: too much screen time, or exposure to bad content? Both matter. But science, the courts, and now lawmakers are converging on a different target: the product's design.

A screen is a window. Content is what passes through it. Design is the machinery that decides what comes through, how fast, for how long, and whether a child can ever walk away.

What California just did

On September 10, Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a package of child online-safety bills (1). The centerpiece, AB 1709, takes effect January 1, 2027, and bars platforms from offering users under 16 addictive features such as infinite scroll, autoplay, and feeds that learn from their behavior to keep them engaged. SB 1119, “Adam’s Law,” requires companion chatbots to follow crisis protocols when a minor expresses suicidal thoughts and to undergo annual independent safety audits. Other bills pause AI chatbot toys and target AI-generated child sexual abuse material.

California isn’t alone. New York’s SAFE for Kids Act will restrict algorithmic feeds for minors starting in 2027 (2). Utah and Alabama have passed laws requiring app stores to verify users’ ages, and Idaho, Oregon, and Washington enacted companion-chatbot laws this year (3).

Notice what these laws don’t do. They don’t ban phones or police opinions. They regulate addictive design features.

Prevention is cheaper than litigation

In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and YouTube negligent in a case brought by a young woman who began using their platforms as a child. The case centered on design, not on what users posted. About 2,000 similar cases are pending (4).

In August, Meta settled with state attorneys general mid-trial for roughly $17 billion (subject to court approval), without admitting wrongdoing. Read the terms, and you’ll find a design document: no like counts on minors’ posts, a nighttime block, notifications silenced during school hours, an optional non-personalized feed (5).

Building those fixes in from the start would likely have cost far less, and spared children harm that no settlement can refund.

The machinery of compulsion

Let's look at how design breeds compulsive behavior.

  • Variable reward. Dopamine neurons fire most for rewards we don’t see coming (6). A feed that’s occasionally wonderful works like a slot machine: maybe the next swipe will be great. A post every now and then receiving some unexplained attention (likes, shares) is what I mean by variable reward. It makes being famous a possibility, even if extremely unlikely. Like the gambler's fallacy, a teen often overestimates the likelihood of their content going viral: "my next one is gonna be viral!"
  • No stopping cues. Infinite scroll and autoplay make continuing the default, and stopping falls to a prefrontal cortex still under construction. Continuing takes less effort and friction than stopping.
  • Opaque personalization. Algorithms learn what holds each child’s attention, often outrage, fear, or insecurity, and serve more. Even these platforms' engineers can’t fully explain why a given video lands in a given feed.
  • Social scorekeeping. Likes and streaks turn belonging into a public number. A developing nervous system needs genuine belonging to develop normally.

Personalization isn’t the villain. A good librarian personalizes and recommends books you may like. The harm comes when it’s optimized for engagement instead of well-being, and for nurturing vulnerabilities instead of protecting them.

Adolescence: the impressionable window

Adolescence is the brain’s second remodeling developmental period. Reward and social systems grow highly responsive around puberty; self-control circuits keep maturing into the mid-20s. Teens who view photos with more likes show stronger activity in the brain’s reward hub (8), and habitual checking in early adolescence has been linked to changes in brain sensitivity to anticipated social feedback (9).

In a study of more than 4,000 youths, high or rising compulsive use of social media was linked to more than twice the risk of suicidal behaviors, while total screen time was not (10).

Safety is an asymmetrical responsibility

We don’t ask children to inspect their car seats or test playground equipment. Adults are entrusted with children, and greater power and knowledge bring a greater duty. Expecting a 13-year-old to out-regulate a team of engineers isn’t empowerment; it’s abdication.

Deepfakes deepen mistrust

Kids are growing up in a century already marked by uncertainty and eroding trust; Americans’ trust in the news media hit a record low of 28% in 2025 (11). Generative AI adds a new layer: when anything can be faked, including sexualized images of classmates, nothing is automatically believable, and real evidence can be dismissed as fake, a problem legal scholars call the “liar’s dividend” (12).

Psychologist George Slavich’s Social Safety Theory proposes that childhood and adolescence are when we form lasting beliefs about whether others are sincere or manipulative (13). For a developing brain, “people can’t be trusted” isn’t an abstract lesson. It becomes a chronic mindset and the spine of their adult nervous system. It becomes the lens through which they interpret the people and world around them.

Stress that never ends

Stress isn’t the enemy. Firdaus Dhabhar, then at Stanford, described how short-term stress, lasting minutes to hours, can enhance immune protection, while long-term stress suppresses it and fuels low-grade chronic inflammation (14). And chronic low-grade inflammation is an ingredient in many chronic diseases.

The difference is recovery. We are well engineered to handle short-term stressors. A healthy stress response rises, peaks, and returns to baseline. A 24/7 stream of graphic news, comparison, and conflict never lets it settle. Stressors ride on top of each other. The baseline gets lost or even shifts.

In lab studies of repeated stress, cortisol responses usually habituate by the second exposure, but inflammatory responses show no sign of habituation (15). Chronic stress is also linked to glucocorticoid resistance, when the body’s brake on inflammation stops working well (16). Slavich notes that imagined or symbolic social threats can activate the same immune defenses that evolved for physical danger. In adolescents, daily social threat combined with short sleep predicted more pro-inflammatory gene expression (13).

Even personality bends. In a 2026 experiment, induced stress lowered people’s momentary agreeableness and conscientiousness and raised neuroticism (17). A teen under constant stress may, day after day, show up as less like themselves.

Repeated hits, no recovery, rising inflammation: a recipe for chronic stress-related illness.

What should change

Here are some suggestions for things designers should change:

  • Design for endings: make finite feeds, remove default autoplay, and add quiet hours.
  • Optimize for well-being, not watch time, with algorithms explainable to parents and regulators. The algorithms must be explained and not remain mystical!
  • Put responsibility where the power is: on companies, which can be enforced by adults in charge of children.
  • Protect recovery: keep phones off during sleep, because sleep is essential to recovering from stress.
  • Batch notifications: Every ping pulls a child out of the present moment, and the mind is drawn back to unfinished business (18). An unopened notification is exactly that. Even notifications people never check disrupt attention (19). In a two-week experiment, adults who received notifications in three daily batches reported better attention, less stress, and better mood, while switching notifications off entirely raised anxiety (20).

The new laws will certainly face backlash in the form of concerns about privacy and free speech. But our children are entrusted to us. They can't audit an algorithm, read a terms-of-service agreement, or argue their case in a courtroom. They are counting on the adults around them to do it for them. Every childhood we shield from a product built to capture it is a mind left free to rest, to trust, to connect, and to grow. So let's protect the children entrusted to us, because in doing so, we protect our future.
